exercise:
Pick any real multi-paragraph document you have on disk (a README, a log file, a PDF you can copy text from). Split it into fixed 500-character chunks with no overlap and count by hand how many chunk boundaries land in the middle of a sentence, a code block, or a table row. Report the percentage, this is your own answer to the folklore number in today's lesson, not someone else's benchmark.

Do the compounding-failure arithmetic yourself with your own guessed numbers for a system you might build: pick a plausible P(chunk intact), P(retrieved in top-k), and P(faithfully used) for your domain, multiply them, and write down which single stage you'd improve first to move the product the most.

Write one sentence for each of the five pipeline stages naming the one thing that would have to go wrong there for a user-facing wrong answer to appear, this is the checklist you'll actually reach for on day 81.
html:
A pipeline, not a spell

Day 1 gave you the open-book-exam framing: instead of asking a model to answer from memory, you hand it a shortlist of passages and let it read them at query time. That framing is correct but it hides the engineering. RAG is not one component, it's a pipeline with five stages, and you already know from every data system you've built that pipelines fail at stage boundaries, not in the middle of a stage. Today's job is to name the five stages and the one or two ways each of them actually breaks in production, so that when your RAG system gives a wrong answer next month you have a mental map of where to start looking instead of poking at the prompt.

The stages, in order:

  1. Ingest & chunk, raw documents become bounded text units.
  2. Embed, each chunk becomes a vector.
  3. Index, vectors become a searchable structure.
  4. Retrieve, a query vector finds nearby chunks.
  5. Assemble & generate, retrieved chunks plus the query become a prompt, and the LLM produces an answer.

Think of it the way you'd think about a write path and a read path in a storage system. Stages 1–3 are the write path: they run once (or on a schedule) and their output is a durable artifact, the index, that many queries will later depend on. Stages 4–5 are the read path: they run per-query, under a latency budget, against whatever the write path already committed. A bug in the write path is silent and systemic, it corrupts every subsequent read the same way, like a bad compaction. A bug in the read path is per-request and noisy. This distinction matters more than almost anything else in RAG debugging, and we'll lean on it again on day 81 when you build a systematic debugging process for bad answers.

Stage 1, Ingest & chunk

A 40-page PDF cannot be embedded as one unit, you'll see the dimensionality argument on day 9, but the short version is that a single vector has to represent the whole document, and averaging away 40 pages of meaning into one point destroys almost all of it. So you cut documents into chunks, typically a few hundred tokens each (day 7 defines token precisely; day 6 covers chunk sizing). The native failure here is boundary damage: a fixed-size character or token window doesn't know where a sentence, a table row, or a code block ends, so a naive splitter routinely cuts a claim from its qualifier, or a function signature from its body. The chunk that gets embedded and later retrieved is missing exactly the words that would have made it useful. This isn't a rare edge case, on real documents (contracts, API docs, log files) naive fixed-window chunking damages a meaningful fraction of boundaries, often double digits as a percentage of chunks, though the exact number is corpus-dependent and nobody has a clean benchmark for it across document types; treat any single quoted number here as folklore until you measure your own corpus, which is exactly what today's exercise asks you to do.

Stage 2, Embed

Each chunk goes through an encoder and comes out as a dense vector, usually 384 to 3072 real numbers. The failure mode here is domain mismatch: embedding models are trained on some distribution of text, mostly web and book text for general-purpose models, and if your chunks are dense with part numbers, SQL, log timestamps, or legal citations, the model has never learned to separate "invoice #48213" from "invoice #48214" in vector space, because during training those two strings were functionally interchangeable noise. You won't see this failure in a demo with clean prose. You'll see it the day someone asks your system to find one specific ticket ID among ten thousand similar ones and the model returns five plausible-looking but wrong tickets. Day 32 is entirely about this failure and what to do about it, spoiler: you don't fix it with a better embedding model, you fix it by not relying on dense vectors alone for exact identifiers.

Stage 3, Index

Vectors get organized into a structure that supports fast approximate nearest-neighbor search, brute force cosine similarity over millions of vectors is an O(n) scan per query, which is fine at ten thousand vectors and a non-starter at ten million. The failure mode here is the one every storage engineer already has intuition for: it's a recall/latency/memory tradeoff, not a free lunch. Approximate indexes (HNSW, IVF, and their compressed variants, days 17 through 27 build several from scratch) trade a small, tunable amount of recall for large gains in speed and memory. The trap is that this tradeoff is invisible until you measure it: an index built with sloppy parameters can silently drop your true top-5 result to rank 40, and nothing in your logs will tell you, because the query still returns fast and returns something. This is why day 14's checkpoint has you actually measure recall against brute force, not just eyeball whether the answers look reasonable.

Stage 4, Retrieve

The query gets embedded with the same encoder and the index returns its nearest neighbors. The subtle failure here, you'll spend all of day 13 on it, is query/passage asymmetry: a question ("how do I configure retries?") and the sentence that answers it ("the client retries with exponential backoff up to five attempts") don't share much surface vocabulary and aren't even the same speech act, so a model that only learned to match similar sentences to each other can rank the right passage below several irrelevant ones that merely repeat the word "retry" more often. Whether your encoder was trained to handle this asymmetry is a training-data question, not a model-size question, and it's the single most common silent bug in home-grown RAG systems.

Stage 5, Assemble & generate

The top-k chunks get concatenated into a prompt with the query, and the LLM generates. Two independent failure modes live here: the model can ignore or misweight passages depending on where they sit in the context window (day 54, "lost in the middle"), and the model can generate a claim that sounds like it came from the passages but doesn't follow from them, hallucination layered on top of correct retrieval, which is why day 63 treats faithfulness as its own measurable thing, separate from whether retrieval worked at all.

Why this compounds multiplicatively

Here's the systems point that makes stage-by-stage thinking non-optional: these failure rates don't add, they multiply, the same way independent stage reliabilities do in any pipeline.

P(correct answer) ≈ P(chunk intact) × P(retrieved in top-k) × P(faithfully used)

e.g. 0.90 × 0.85 × 0.92 ≈ 0.70

Three stages, each individually looking pretty good, compound to a system that's wrong roughly three times in ten. This is exactly why "just use a better LLM" so often fails to move the needle, stage 5 is only one of three multiplicands, and if stages 1–4 are the weak links, a stronger generator just hallucinates more confidently on the same bad context. Diagnosing which stage is actually your bottleneck, instead of guessing, is the whole subject of Phase 4 starting day 56.

Next

Day 3 goes down to the representation layer itself: why raw text can't be searched at all, and the string-to-number conversion that every stage above is quietly built on top of.
summary: RAG is five stages bolted together, chunk, embed, index, retrieve, generate, and end-to-end quality is the product of each stage's success rate, not the average. Today we trace the pipeline as a data flow and catalog the specific failure mode native to each stage.
title: The pipeline end to end, and where it breaks
